Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction

Prakhar Kaushik    Soumava Paul    Alan Yuille Affiliation: CCVL, Johns Hopkins University
Abstract

Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31×2.31\times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.

keywords
Surface elements, hexagonal primitives, novel view synthesis, surface reconstruction, image representation

1 Introduction

Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have progressed rapidly, from neural radiance fields [25] to explicit Gaussian primitives that render in real time [18] to surface aligned planar primitives like 2DGS [14], and Triangle Splatting [13]. These methods differ in geometry, but all face the same question: how much of the scene can one primitive represent, and at what cost? This has led to the search for an overarching universal primitive which is efficient, expressive, and retains high geometric fidelity. This is even more important in resource-constrained settings, where efficiency includes not only rendering speed and model size but also the memory required during training. Previous methods have often traded one aspect for another. For example, conventional Gaussian and triangle splats typically represent one view-conditioned color per primitive, so spatial variation emerges through many overlapping elements, leading to large overdraw. Others like BBSplat [33] add per-primitive textures, or use shared neural appearance fields like NeST [39] and Nexels [30]. These methods increase per-element capacity, but move complexity into textures, grids, or decoders. In contrast, we target the entire quality–efficiency trade-off at the primitive itself. For resource-constrained settings, this efficiency includes not only rendering speed and model size, but also the memory required during training.

At constrained representation budgets, we seek a balance between geometric fidelity and appearance expressivity. Since agreement with training images alone does not guarantee accurate geometry [36], we therefore target both surface reconstruction accuracy and novel-view rendering quality within a compact surface primitive.

We are motivated by the idea that natural images and scenes are highly structured: large regions are often locally planar with smoothly varying appearance. An efficient surface primitive should therefore be able to exploit this underlying structure, wherever possible, and do so in a compact and self-contained manner.

We introduce Hexels, planar surface elements that combine a hexagonal support with a first-order spatial color field. Natural scenes contain large regions that are locally simple in geometry and appearance; a Hexel can represent such a region with one large primitive, including smooth color variation within it, while smaller Hexels capture boundaries, curvature, and fine detail. This directly targets redundancy in surface-aligned splatting: rather than approximating structured regions with many overlapping, spatially constant primitives, Hexels increase what each primitive can represent.

Why a hexagon? Regular hexagons tile a plane without gaps and cover more area for the same boundary length than triangles or squares (other tileable primitives) [9] (discussed in Appendix G). When combined with the local color field, each Hexel can model both the region itself and smooth appearance variation within it. In 3D, Hexels are rendered as oriented surface elements using perspective-correct ray-plane intersection and depth-ordered blending. The same primitive can be placed directly in the image plane for 2D image representation. Thus, Hexels provide a single compact primitive family for novel-view synthesis, surface reconstruction, and image representation, without requiring texture maps, neural appearance fields, or decoding networks.

We evaluate Hexels for 3D novel view synthesis (memory-matched, primitive-matched, and unconstrained), surface reconstruction, and 2D image representation. We primarily use 34 scenes across DTU [16], Tanks and Temples [21], and Mip-NeRF360 [1]. At matched model sizes, Hexels improves PSNR over 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB with upto 3.6×3.6\times less VRAM requirements and over Triangle Splatting by 1.70–2.90 dB, with up to 1.87×1.87\times higher rendering FPS (Table 2). At matched primitive budgets, Hexels improves PSNR over 2DGS by up to 4.74 dB, using 1.761.76–1.95×1.95\times less model size and upto 7×7\times less VRAM, and renders up to 2.31×2.31\times faster (Table 3). Under unrestricted model sizes, Hexels still improve PSNR over 2DGS by 0.90 dB on both Tanks and Temples and DTU, while rendering 1.37×1.37\times and 2.26×2.26\times faster, respectively. For surface reconstruction, Hexels achieves 0.978 mm mean Chamfer distance over 15 DTU scans, versus 1.375 mm for 2DGS at the same model-memory budget (Table 5). On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, mean F1 for Hexels is 34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS (Table 6). Hexels also converges faster (Figure 3) and improves 2D image representation over Image-GS [40] (Table 1).

Contributions.

  • •

    Compact Hexel primitive. We introduce Hexels, compact, self-contained surface primitives for resource-constrained rendering and reconstruction, combining efficient hexagonal support with a first-order local color field without textures, feature grids, neural decoders, or baking.

  • •

    Strong quality-efficiency trade-offs. Under matched primitive budgets, Hexels outperform 2DGS by 2.08–4.74 dB while using 2×2\times less learned storage per primitive, upto 7×7\times lower peak training VRAM, and up to 2.31×2.31\times higher rendering throughput. Under matched model-memory budgets, they improve PSNR by 4.53–7.38 dB while using upto 3.6×3.6\times lower peak training VRAM and rendering up to 1.87×1.87\times faster.

  • •

    One primitive across tasks. The same representation applies across novel-view synthesis, surface reconstruction, and 2D image representation, achieving strong performance and efficiency without changing the underlying primitive.

2 Related Work

Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have improved rapidly since NeRF [25], which represents scenes as neural fields of density and view-dependent radiance. Feature grids and explicit encodings reduced their training and rendering cost [26, 6], while 3DGS [18] replaced neural fields with explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time rasterization. 2DGS [14] further replaced volumetric Gaussians with planar surfels, substantially improving surface reconstruction. These advances made rendering faster and geometry more accurate, but efficient representation requires more: high quality together with low model storage, low training VRAM, few primitives, and high FPS. Appendix H discusses these trade-offs.

Subsequent work improves different parts of this trade-off, but usually with a catch. Triangle Splatting [13], Deformable Beta Splatting [23], and 3D Convex Splatting [11] redesign the primitive or kernel to improve expressiveness or rendering speed, but at cost of higher memory and VRAM usage. Hybrid methods such as BBSplat [33], NeST [39], and Nexels [30] reduce geometric redundancy by separating geometry from appearance through textures or neural fields; this shifts capacity into additional memory, training state, and computation. Other methods retrofit existing representations through pruning, parameter sharing, quantization, distillation, or baking  [19, 24, 5, 2] but still largely struggled to address the efficiency problem on all of its axes. Hexels provides a solution to the efficiency problem by redesigning the primitive itself to exploit local structure and geometry in appearance. The resulting primitive is compact in the form in which it is learned and rendered, simultaneously targeting storage, training VRAM, primitive count, FPS, and reconstruction quality. Further, unlike previous works, Hexels are general surface primitives: the same underlying design applies directly to oriented 3D surfaces and to 2D images without major changes to the representation or optimization.

3 Hexels: Hexagonal Surface Elements

We introduce Hexels, planar hexagonal surface elements designed to reduce overlap and overdraw, avoid the long tails of Gaussian footprints, and represent more appearance within each primitive. Each Hexel combines a soft hexagonal support with a first-order spatial color field, allowing a single primitive to cover a larger coherent surface region while modeling smooth appearance variation within it. In 3D, a Hexel is an oriented planar patch with a local 2D coordinate system. Following 2DGS [14], we evaluate each primitive at the perspective-correct ray-plane intersection and blend the resulting contributions in depth order.

Modeling

A Hexel (Figure 1) is centered at \bpi∈ℝ3\bp_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} with two orthogonal unit tangent directions \btu,i\bt_{u,i} and \btv,i\bt_{v,i} and positive tangent scales su,is_{u,i} and sv,is_{v,i}. A local point (u,v)(u,v) maps to world space as

Pi​(u,v)=\bpi+su,i​\btu,i​u+sv,i​\btv,i​v.P_{i}(u,v)=\bp_{i}+s_{u,i}\bt_{u,i}u+s_{v,i}\bt_{v,i}v. (1)

The tangent directions are obtained from a normalized quaternion, with \bni=\btu,i×\btv,i\bn_{i}=\bt_{u,i}\times\bt_{v,i} defining the surface normal. This maps the hexagon to an oriented, anisotropically scaled planar patch in 3D.

Hexagonal support.

In the local plane, we define

d⁡(u,v)=max⁡{|v|,|32​u+12​v|,|32​u−12​v|}−1.d(u,v)=\max\left\{|v|,\left|\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}u+\tfrac{1}{2}v\right|,\left|\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}u-\tfrac{1}{2}v\right|\right\}-1. (2)

The contour d⁡(u,v)=0d(u,v)=0 defines the canonical regular hexagon, with d<0d<0 inside and d>0d>0 outside. We convert this into a soft support weight

Ki​(u,v)=σ⁡(−βi​d​(u,v)),σ⁡(a)=11+exp⁡(−a),K_{i}(u,v)=\sigma\!\left(-\beta_{i}d(u,v)\right),\qquad\sigma(a)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-a)}, (3)

where βi>0\beta_{i}>0 controls edge sharpness. Increasing βi\beta_{i} produces a sharper transition around the hexagon while preserving the Ki=1/2K_{i}=1/2 contour. The scales in Eq. (1) control the spatial extent of the support, while the rasterizer truncates negligible sigmoid tails below its contribution threshold (See Appendix A for details).

We use a hexagon because it provides an efficient, nearly isotropic way to cover a plane. Regular hexagons tile a plane without gaps and, at equal area, require less perimeter than regular triangles or squares, consistent with the honeycomb theorem [9]. More concretely, under the local first-order approximation model of Appendix G, a suitably oriented and anisotropically scaled hexagon can cover about 30%30\% more area than the corresponding square and twice the area of the corresponding triangle for the same bounded color error (See Proposition G.3). Our results reflect that these ideas do help structure a more efficient primitive even in non-ideal settings.

Spatial appearance.

We model appearance within each Hexel using a first-order color field:

\bcisp​(u,v)=\bc0,i+u​\bgu,i+v​\bgv,i,\bc_{i}^{\mathrm{sp}}(u,v)=\bc_{0,i}+u\bg_{u,i}+v\bg_{v,i}, (4)

where \bc0,i\bc_{0,i} is the base RGB color and \bgu,i,\bgv,i\bg_{u,i},\bg_{v,i} are RGB gradients along the two local coordinates. This allows one Hexel to represent smooth appearance variation across its surface rather than assigning a single spatial color to the primitive. Since the field is defined in local coordinates, increasing a tangent scale spreads the same color variation over a larger physical region. We refer to this view-independent model as V1, with 20 learned parameters per Hexel, compared with 58 for the evaluated 2DGS primitive. Our V2 variant adds compact view dependence through a linear residual \bri​(\bdi)=Ai​\bdi\br_{i}(\bd_{i})=A_{i}\bd_{i}, where \bdi\bd_{i} is the normalized direction from the camera center to the Hexel center, for 29 parameters in total. We also consider an optional V3 variant that replaces the linear residual with degree-three spherical harmonics. See Appendix A.1 for the complete parameterization details.

Splatting.

Following 2DGS, we recover local coordinates (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}) at each pixel using perspective-correct ray–plane intersection and composite primitives front-to-back in depth order. A Hexel contributes αi=min⁡{oi​Ki​(ui,vi),0.99}\alpha_{i}=\min\{o_{i}K_{i}(u_{i},v_{i}),0.99\}, with color evaluated from its local appearance field at (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}). Thus, relative to 2DGS, the rasterization and compositing remain unchanged; we replace the Gaussian weight with the Hexel support and evaluate spatially varying color within each primitive. Implementation details are given in Appendix B.

Training.

We optimize all Hexel parameters directly from calibrated training images with Adam [20], using the standard photometric objective ℒ=(1−λ)​‖I^−I‖1+λ⁡(1−SSIM⁡(I^,I))\mathcal{L}=(1-\lambda)\|\hat{I}-I\|_{1}+\lambda(1-\operatorname{SSIM}(\hat{I},I)). Hexels are initialized from either sparse COLMAP points [31] or, where stated, a denser MVS reconstruction [32] obtained from the training views. Unless otherwise specified, our reported models use a fixed primitive population.

Densification and Pruning.

For unconstrained training, we additionally consider standard densification and pruning, following 3DGS and 2DGS. Primitives with large position gradients are cloned or split, with new Hexels initialized near the parent in its tangent plane. We conservatively prune mature primitives that make negligible contributions across the training views. More details are given in Appendix C.

At inference, we precompute camera-independent quantities and use an RGB-only rasterizer; depth ordering and compositing are unchanged from the training renderer. Full implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

3.1 Representing 2D Images as Hexels

Unlike most 3D surface primitives, Hexels are general and can be used directly for both 3D scenes and 2D images. For efficient image representation, a 2D Hexel is defined by its image-plane center \bmi\bm_{i}, rotation θi\theta_{i}, two scales sx,i,sy,is_{x,i},s_{y,i}, and support sharpness βi\beta_{i}. The same hexagonal support from Eq. (2) is evaluated directly at each pixel, without projection, ray–plane intersection, opacity, or depth ordering. Let \bSi=diag⁡(sx,i,sy,i)\bS_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(s_{x,i},s_{y,i}) be the positive scale matrix and \bR​(θi)\bR(\theta_{i}) the planar rotation. For a pixel \bx\bx, we compute

\bui=\bSi−1​\bR​(θi)⊤​(\bmi−\bx),wi​(\bx)=σ⁡(−βi​d​(\bui)),\bu_{i}=\bS_{i}^{-1}\bR(\theta_{i})^{\top}(\bm_{i}-\bx),\qquad w_{i}(\bx)=\sigma\!\left(-\beta_{i}d(\bu_{i})\right),

Here wi​(\bx)w_{i}(\bx) is a blending weight: it is larger inside the Hexel’s footprint and decreases smoothly outside it. Following Image-GS [40], each pixel retains up to K=10K=10 Hexels with the largest weights among those assigned to its tile. Let 𝒮K​(\bx)\mathcal{S}_{K}(\bx) be the indices of these selected Hexels. Their RGB colors \bci​(\bx)\bc_{i}(\bx) form a weighted average:

\bc​(\bx)=∑i∈𝒮K​(\bx)wi​(\bx)​\bci​(\bx)∑i∈𝒮K​(\bx)wi​(\bx)+ϵ.\bc(\bx)=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{K}(\bx)}w_{i}(\bx)\bc_{i}(\bx)}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{K}(\bx)}w_{i}(\bx)+\epsilon}.

ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4} prevents division by zero.

We use the first-order spatial color field as the primary 2D appearance model, expressed in image coordinates; constant-color Hexels, with a fixed shared β\beta, match Image-GS’s eight stored scalars per primitive. Both methods use image-gradient-based initialization from [40] and an L1 plus SSIM loss. Image-GS retains its original training, densification, and pruning methodology. Appendix D provides more training and inference details.

This 2D representation setting permits a straightforward way to evaluate overdraw using reconstruction error and primitive overlap. On the 45-image Image-GS benchmark, Hexels improve PSNR from 33.16 to 35.82 dB and reduce LPIPS from .1372 to .0924 over ImageGS. They use 5.1K rather than 10K iterations and 157.07 rather than 238.40 seconds of image fitting/training time (Table 1). Even using constant-color instead of linear color representation, Hexels still improve all three quality metrics, fit in 112.11 seconds, and occupy 289.799 kB memory, versus 292.175 kB for Image-GS. Figure 2 shows qualitative comparisons.

4 Experiments

We evaluate novel-view synthesis under matched model memory, matched primitive budgets and native baseline settings. As our focus is on fundamental parameter-based efficiency, all Hexels results do not utilize any post-quantization or compression. For initial runtime compression analysis, refer to Appendix I.3.

Implementation.

Hexels start from sparse COLMAP points and train for 30K iterations. Fixed configurations retain the initial population; densified configurations use mixed clone/split growth and contribution-based pruning, with a 2M limit.

Appendix I.2 reports all configurations. Training and evaluation details are in Appendix E.1.

Datasets, baselines, and metrics.

We evaluate nine Mip-NeRF360 scenes [1], fifteen DTU scans [16], and ten Tanks and Temples scenes [21], using common held-out views and resolutions. We report PSNR, SSIM [34], LPIPS [37], training time, peak training VRAM, rendering FPS, and deployment memory size, averaged over scenes. Our baselines are 3DGS [18], 3D Convex Splatting [11], BBSplat [33], Nexels [30], 2DGS [14], Triangle Splatting [13], and MeshSplatting [12]. Tables group methods into volumetric primitives, textured or neural surfels, and native surface-aligned primitives with local appearance. We select these baselines as competitive representatives of their respective classes, spanning complementary quality-efficiency trade-offs. The final group - 2DGS, Triangle Splatting, and MeshSplatting - provides the closest comparison to Hexels, as these methods use explicit surface-aligned primitives without separate texture maps or neural appearance fields; we therefore emphasize this group in our analysis. To our knowledge, this evaluation over 34 real-world scenes is the largest quantitative NVS evaluation, by scene count, among the original papers introducing the compared methods.

4.1 Novel View Synthesis

Matched memory.

Like BBSplat’s fixed-storage comparisons [33], we constrain baseline primitive counts and other learned components to compare methods under matched uncompressed model-memory budgets. Table 2 compares all methods at the V1 model-memory budget along with corresponding training resources and rendering rates; additional comparisons at the V2 and V3 budgets are provided in Appendix I.1. At matched model-memory budgets, Hexels V1 improves PSNR over 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB and over Triangle Splatting by 1.70–2.90 dB across the three benchmarks. Average rendering speed (FPS) range from 377.8 to 830.8 FPS, or 1.541.54–1.87×1.87\times those of 2DGS. On Mip-NeRF360, the mean PSNR gain is 6.99 dB. All these improvements come with upto 3.6×3.6\times less VRAM usage than 2DGS. Figure 4 shows that Hexels retain fine scene structure under these compact memory budgets. This matched-memory evaluation is our primary efficiency setting, in which Hexels establish the strongest overall quality–efficiency trade-off among the evaluated methods. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix E.1.

Matched primitive budget.

We use this equal-primitive experiment to ablate the Hexel primitive design as a whole under an equal primitive population ceiling. Table 3 uses each scene’s SfM point count as the common budget across all methods. Hexel V1/V2 provide compact alternatives, while V3 uses a richer appearance model with a larger per-primitive memory cost. V3 outperforms 2DGS, Triangle Splatting, and MeshSplatting in mean PSNR across all three datasets. V3 exceeds Triangle Splatting in mean PSNR by 0.68 dB on Mip-NeRF360, 2.82 dB on DTU and 0.88 dB on Tanks and Temples. Hexels remain the most efficient primitives amongst all compared surface alignment methods. While we find that BBSplat sometimes outperforms Hexels, it comes at the expense of all relevant efficiency metrics, including training time, FPS, VRAM, and memory, as it requires a separate appearance model and therefore belongs to a separate primitive category. Figure 4 shows the detail retained by Hexels under this common primitive budget. At the same primitive budget, Hexels V2 outperforms 2DGS on all quality metrics across all three datasets, improving PSNR by up to 4.74 dB while using up to 7×7\times lower peak training VRAM, 1.76–1.95×\times less deployment memory, and rendering up to 2.31×\times faster.

Native baselines.

Although unconstrained training is not the primary focus of our efficiency-oriented evaluation, we also compare against all baselines in their native settings in Table 4. This tests whether Hexels remain competitive when model memory and primitive count are unrestricted. On Mip-NeRF360, densified V3 is within 0.30 dB of 2DGS while rendering 2.06×2.06\times faster and using 2.00×2.00\times less deployment memory. On DTU and T&T, it improves PSNR over 2DGS by 0.90 and 0.90 dB, respectively, while rendering 2.26×2.26\times and 1.37×1.37\times faster. Hexel (FP32 deployment) memory is 27.03 MB versus 56.20 MB for 2DGS on DTU, and 198.84 MB versus 177.56 MB on T&T. BBSplat remains 0.50 dB better on DTU, while 3D Convex Splatting is 0.27 dB better on T&T; however, neither provides a direct comparison to Hexels as a native surface-aligned primitive. The fixed V2 variant provides the corresponding lower-cost yet high-performance alternative. In fact, for comparative visual quality, V2 uses upto 14×14\times less peak VRAM during training and upto 34×34\times less memory during inference compared to 2DGS. Figure 5 compares densified V3 with the native/unconstrained baselines on Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks and Temples scenes.

Across 34 scenes, Hexels consistently achieve a strong quality–efficiency trade-off. In our primary matched-memory setting, Hexels outperform every evaluated baseline in PSNR, including volumetric and textured or neural representations. We further evaluate the primitive design as a whole under the same primitive-count budget. In this setting, Hexels outperform all evaluated native surface-aligned methods while using substantially less training VRAM and, for V1/V2, less deployment/inference storage memory; Hexels also achieves the highest FPS on each dataset. Finally, Hexels remain competitive in the native unconstrained setting, where the fixed and densified variants together provide the strongest overall quality–efficiency trade-off among the evaluated native surface-aligned representations.

4.2 Efficient Surface Reconstruction

We further evaluate surface reconstruction on all 15 DTU scans and 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes. As can be seen from the results (Table 5), our primary comparison is with 2DGS, and our primary setting is memory-matched and primitive-matched as before, while we also report unconstrained results. Table 5 reports mean DTU Chamfer distance (CD). Hexels reaches 0.978 mm, compared with 1.375 mm and 1.449 mm for the memory- and primitive-controlled 2DGS variants. Triangle Splatting and MeshSplatting obtain 1.124 mm and 1.662 mm, respectively. Unconstrained 2DGS achieves 0.794 mm, however trails Hexels in memory usage which use 0.61 GiB mean peak training VRAM, versus 1.02 GiB and 0.98 GiB for the two memory/primitive matched 2DGS variants. Notably, Hexels in Table 5 are fixed, whereas other methods allow densification and pruning even beyond the final memory/primitive capacity. We report further improvements in surface reconstruction with densification for Hexels in Appendix F. In summary, Hexels retain substantially better surface geometry for the same model memory and even the same number of primitives.

On Tanks and Temples, Table 6 reports the average of the 6 scene-wise F1 scores at the official thresholds. Hexels achieves 34.38%, versus 31.72% for unconstrained 2DGS, and 22.05% and 21.03% for our main memory- and primitive-controlled settings, followed by 18.63% for Triangle Splatting and 27.13% for MeshSplatting.

Figure 6 shows qualitative results of surface reconstruction. Hexels demonstrate reduced wall holes and surface fragmentation despite using significantly less VRAM and memory.

4.3 Applications

Direct Surface-Cell Extraction

Hexels provide an explicit surface representation that can be exported definably and in constant time after optimization from images. Unlike the depth-fusion pipeline used for mesh extraction in 2DGS [14], this conversion requires no depth rendering, voxel grid, or Marching Cubes. The resulting surface cells can be used directly in object-centric applications such as 3D generation, segmentation, and representation learning, which we leave to future work.

For each retained Hexel, we transform the six vertices of its canonical hexagon, defined by d=0d=0, into world space using Eq. (1). Connecting consecutive vertices produces six edges and one polygonal face. Colors are obtained from the base RGB or evaluated from the spatial color field. Each cell remains associated with its parent Hexel, providing direct access to its geometry and appearance, for any downstream application-based optimization, as the associated Position and parameters remain differentiable with respect to the task.

The conversion requires O⁡(1)O(1) work per Hexel. The exported cells can be optimized independently, opening avenues for many downstream applications in both 3D and 4D. Figure 7 shows the resulting wireframes and surface cells. More details in Appendix E.5.

Resource-constrained reconstruction.

Compact, fixed-population Hexels retain high reconstruction quality while requiring little model memory and training VRAM and supporting fast rendering. These gains arise directly from the primitive and do not rely on texture atlases, neural decoders, pruning, or quantization. This makes Hexels well suited to reconstruction and rendering on memory-limited and edge devices. Pruning and quantization remain optional extensions that could further reduce deployment storage.

We have also developed an efficient renderer that directly evaluates the same Hexel representation used during training, without baking or conversion to a separate deployment representation. We will release it together with the training code. This provides a direct path toward on-device NVS and surface reconstruction, where captured images and reconstructed scene data can remain local to the device.

4.4 Additional Ablation

To further isolate the effects of Hexel’s shape and spatial appearance, we ablate Gaussian and hexagonal shape supports with constant RGB color or first-order RGB gradients (Hexel V1). We use planar image fitting for our ablation instead of a 3D scene to keep surface normals and depth order fixed, therefore avoiding confounding changes in reconstructed geometry and multiview visibility. All four settings of our ablation use the same primitive count, initialization, loss (MSE), and optimization (6K-step Adam).

This differs from the Image-GS comparison in Section 3.1, which uses normalized top-KK blending and quantization-aware training. The objective here is to do one-to-one analysis of shape and appearance.

Figure 8 compares the four ablative settings on flat and smoothly shaded targets with 256 primitives. At either appearance model, Hexels achieve higher PSNR than Gaussians on both targets, isolating the effect of support shape. Adding spatial gradients improves both shapes, showing the benefit of using our color gradients within each primitive, and providing support to our motivation for the appearance design. The linear color gradient Hexel achieves the lowest error: on the shaded target, it reaches 37.07 dB versus 35.13 dB for the same appearance Gaussian, while reducing the overdraw - represented using mean blended contributions of primitives from 10.47 to 2.48 per pixel. The error and contribution maps in the figure show these improvements.

Figure 9 shows more results regarding the overdraw benefits for complicated and detailed artworks. Hexels require significantly fewer primitives per pixel (reducing mean blends/pixel contributions by 71–80% relative to their Gaussian counterparts) to achieve similar perceptual quality.

5 Conclusion

We introduced Hexels, a general surface primitive, for 2D and 3D, that exploits the local structure of the data it represents: hexagonal support efficiently covers coherent surface regions, while a first-order spatial color field models appearance variation within each primitive. Across our three 3D benchmarks, Hexels establish a new quality–efficiency frontier among the evaluated surface-aligned representations, improving PSNR by up to 7.38 dB at matched model memory, using lower peak training VRAM and up to 2×\times less learned state at matched primitive count, while rendering up to 2.31×\times faster than 2DGS. The same primitive also performs strongly for memory-constrained surface reconstruction and directly generalizes to efficient 2D image representation. Hexels therefore move efficiency into the primitive itself, opening a path toward high-quality novel-view synthesis and explicit surface reconstruction on edge and resource-constrained hardware.

Limitations and Future Work.

A first-order color model cannot represent arbitrary texture within a single primitive. High-frequency or uncorrelated appearance requires smaller primitives or a richer color model, reducing the expected benefit of exploiting local smoothness. Sparse initialization can also leave parts of a scene poorly covered, and the independent surface cells do not form a watertight mesh. Sharper footprints do not by themselves prevent sampling artifacts, especially at small projected sizes or grazing views. Hexels does not outperform every baseline on every metric; the appendix provides the full comparisons. Our current primitives are planar. A natural extension is developable Hexels: curved patches with zero Gaussian curvature that remain locally isometric to the planar canonical hexagon. Such primitives could bend along one principal direction, for example, as cylindrical or conical patches, while preserving the simple 2D footprint and affine appearance parameterization. This may allow individual primitives to cover larger regions of locally near-developable geometry without introducing additional overlap.

Appendix A Hexel Parameterization

Stored parameters.

A 3D Hexel stores its center \bpi∈ℝ3\bp_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, two positive tangent scales su,is_{u,i} and sv,is_{v,i}, a quaternion defining its orientation, opacity oio_{i}, and support sharpness βi\beta_{i}. The quaternion is normalized before constructing the tangent frame, and its first two axes define the orthogonal tangent directions \btu,i\bt_{u,i} and \btv,i\bt_{v,i}. Thus, the geometric and support parameters require 11 learned scalars: three for position, two for scale, four for orientation, one for opacity, and one for support sharpness.

The V1 appearance model adds a base RGB value and two RGB spatial gradients, for nine additional scalars. A V1 Hexel therefore contains 20 learned scalars in total. V2 adds nine directional coefficients, while V3 adds 45 spherical-harmonic coefficients, giving 29 and 65 learned scalars, respectively.

A.1 Appearance

The spatial appearance field used by all three variants is

\bcisp​(u,v)=\bc0,i+u​\bgu,i+v​\bgv,i,\bc_{i}^{\mathrm{sp}}(u,v)=\bc_{0,i}+u\,\bg_{u,i}+v\,\bg_{v,i}, (5)

where \bc0,i∈ℝ3\bc_{0,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is the base color and \bgu,i,\bgv,i∈ℝ3\bg_{u,i},\bg_{v,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} are RGB gradients along the two local Hexel coordinates. V1 uses this spatial field directly. V2 and V3 add a view-dependent RGB residual:

\bci​(u,v,\bdi)=\bcisp​(u,v)+\bri​(\bdi),\bc_{i}(u,v,\bd_{i})=\bc_{i}^{\mathrm{sp}}(u,v)+\br_{i}(\bd_{i}), (6)

where \bdi\bd_{i} is the normalized world-space direction from the camera center to the Hexel center \bpi\bp_{i}, and

\bri​(\bdi)={0,V1,\bAi​\bdi,V2,∑ℓ=13∑m=−ℓℓ\bai,ℓ​m​Yℓ​m​(\bdi),V3.\br_{i}(\bd_{i})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{V1},\\[2.0pt] \bA_{i}\bd_{i},&\text{V2},\\[4.0pt] \displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\ba_{i,\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\bd_{i}),&\text{V3}.\end{cases} (7)

Here \bAi∈ℝ3×3\bA_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} gives the nine coefficients of the linear V2 residual. For V3, Yℓ​mY_{\ell m} denotes a real spherical-harmonic basis function and \bai,ℓ​m∈ℝ3\ba_{i,\ell m}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} its RGB coefficient. Degrees one through three contain 15 basis functions, giving 45 learned coefficients; the base RGB \bc0,i\bc_{0,i} provides the view-independent constant component.

The viewing direction is evaluated once at the Hexel center. Therefore, for a fixed camera, the V2 and V3 residuals are constant over the primitive: view dependence changes its RGB offset but not the spatial gradients \bgu,i\bg_{u,i} and \bgv,i\bg_{v,i}.

A.2 Derivatives

Support derivatives.

Let \bu=(u,v)⊤\bu=(u,v)^{\top} and define the three unit normals

\bn0=(0,1)⊤,\bn1=(3/2,1/2)⊤,\bn2=(3/2,−1/2)⊤.\bn_{0}=(0,1)^{\top},\quad\bn_{1}=(\sqrt{3}/2,1/2)^{\top},\quad\bn_{2}=(\sqrt{3}/2,-1/2)^{\top}. (8)

Together, 𝒩={±\bn0,±\bn1,±\bn2}\mathcal{N}=\{\pm\bn_{0},\pm\bn_{1},\pm\bn_{2}\} are the outward normals of the six sides of the canonical hexagon. The hexagonal function can therefore be written as

d⁡(\bu)=max\bn∈𝒩⁡\bn⊤​\bu−1=maxe∈{0,1,2}⁡|\bne⊤​\bu|−1.d(\bu)=\max_{\bn\in\mathcal{N}}\bn^{\top}\bu-1=\max_{e\in\{0,1,2\}}|\bn_{e}^{\top}\bu|-1. (9)

Its zero level set defines the canonical hexagonal boundary, with d<0d<0 inside and d>0d>0 outside.

At a point where one projection is strictly larger than the other five, let \bn⋆\bn^{\star} denote the corresponding normal. For sufficiently small changes in \bu\bu, this projection remains the largest, so d⁡(\bu)=\bn⋆⁣⊤​\bu−1d(\bu)=\bn^{\star\top}\bu-1 and

∇\bud=\bn⋆.\nabla_{\bu}d=\bn^{\star}. (10)

When two or more projections tie for the largest value, small movements in different directions can select different side normals. The function remains continuous, but has no ordinary gradient at that point. Any of the tied maximizing normals is a valid subgradient: one of the slopes that can be used for optimization at this corner of the function. These ties form a zero-area set, so the ordinary gradient exists almost everywhere. Although dd gives the exact hexagonal contour and inside-outside sign, it is not the Euclidean signed distance outside the hexagon near its vertices.

For the soft support K⁡(\bu)=σ⁡(−β​d​(\bu))K(\bu)=\sigma(-\beta d(\bu)), the chain rule gives

∇\buK=−β​K​(1−K)​∇\bud,∂K∂β=−d⁡(\bu)​K​(1−K).\nabla_{\bu}K=-\beta K(1-K)\nabla_{\bu}d,\qquad\frac{\partial K}{\partial\beta}=-d(\bu)K(1-K). (11)

The spatial derivative holds wherever dd is differentiable. At a tie, substituting a selected maximizing normal gives the corresponding gradient choice for optimization. The derivative with respect to β\beta exists at every point.

The rendered opacity contribution is α=min⁡{o​K,0.99}\alpha=\min\{oK,0.99\}. For o​K<0.99oK<0.99,

∂α∂o=K,∂α∂K=o.\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial o}=K,\qquad\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial K}=o. (12)

For o​K>0.99oK>0.99, α\alpha is locally constant, and both derivatives are zero. At o​K=0.99oK=0.99, our backward implementation uses the unclamped-branch derivatives.

Color and compositing derivatives.

For the spatial color field, ∂\bcisp/∂u=\bgu,i\partial\bc_{i}^{\mathrm{sp}}/\partial u=\bg_{u,i} and ∂\bcisp/∂v=\bgv,i\partial\bc_{i}^{\mathrm{sp}}/\partial v=\bg_{v,i}. Changes in local coordinates therefore affect both the support weight and the color within the Hexel.

Let \bc>i\bc_{>i} be the color obtained by compositing only the retained Hexels behind primitive ii, including the background and starting with transmittance one. With the retained contributions and their order fixed, let Ti=∏j<i(1−αj)T_{i}=\prod_{j<i}(1-\alpha_{j}) be the transmittance reaching primitive ii. Then

∂\bc​(\bx)∂\bci=Ti​αi​\bI3,∂\bc​(\bx)∂αi=Ti​(\bci−\bc>i),\frac{\partial\bc(\bx)}{\partial\bc_{i}}=T_{i}\alpha_{i}\bI_{3},\qquad\frac{\partial\bc(\bx)}{\partial\alpha_{i}}=T_{i}\bigl(\bc_{i}-\bc_{>i}\bigr), (13)

where \bI3\bI_{3} is the 3×33\times 3 identity matrix. The first expression weights the color derivative by the primitive’s blending weight. The second describes how increasing its opacity replaces some of the color behind it with its own color.

A back-to-front traversal accumulates these derivatives. Gradients propagate to appearance and opacity, and through the local coordinates and ray–plane intersection to geometry. For V2 and V3, moving the Hexel center also changes its view-dependent color. We differentiate through the numerically stabilized view direction \bdi=(\bpi−\bo)/‖\bpi−\bo‖2+10−8\bd_{i}=(\bp_{i}-\bo)/\sqrt{\|\bp_{i}-\bo\|^{2}+10^{-8}}, where \bo\bo is the camera center.

Using 𝜹i=\bpi−\bo\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}=\bp_{i}-\bo and ρi=‖𝜹i‖2+10−8\rho_{i}=\sqrt{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\|^{2}+10^{-8}}, the additional position gradient is

∂\bdi∂\bpi=\bI3ρi−𝜹i​𝜹i⊤ρi3.\frac{\partial\bd_{i}}{\partial\bp_{i}}=\frac{\bI_{3}}{\rho_{i}}-\frac{\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}^{\top}}{\rho_{i}^{3}}. (14)

The V2 variant has Jacobian \bAi\bA_{i} with respect to \bdi\bd_{i}; Hexel V3 has a differentiable polynomial SH basis. Both therefore contribute to the position gradient in addition to the ray–plane geometry.

Optimization coordinates.

For 3D applications, (positive) scales and sharpness parameters are represented exponentially, and opacity is derived using a sigmoid: sa=exp⁡(ℓa)s_{a}=\exp(\ell_{a}), β=exp⁡(b)\beta=\exp(b), and o=σ⁡(a)o=\sigma(a). For a latent or upstream gradient z¯=∂ℒ/∂z\bar{z}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z,

ℓ¯a=sa​s¯a,b¯=β​β¯,a¯=o⁡(1−o)​o¯.\bar{\ell}_{a}=s_{a}\bar{s}_{a},\qquad\bar{b}=\beta\bar{\beta},\qquad\bar{a}=o(1-o)\bar{o}. (15)

For the forward pass, the kernel applies the floor function for sharpness parameter at 10−410^{-4} for numerical stability. Below this value, its backward pass uses the support derivative evaluated at the floor, using a straight-through gradient value.

Appendix B Rasterization

Perspective-correct coordinates.

Like 2DGS [14], we recover local Hexel coordinates through ray–plane intersection. Let \bTi∈ℝ3×3\bT_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} map local homogeneous coordinates (u,v,1)⊤(u,v,1)^{\top} to homogeneous image coordinates, combining Eq. (1) with the calibrated camera. It factors as \bTi=\bPi​\bMi\bT_{i}=\bPi\bM_{i}, where the local-to-world matrix

\bMi\displaystyle\bM_{i} =(su,i​\btu,isv,i​\btv,i\bpi001)∈ℝ4×3,\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}s_{u,i}\bt_{u,i}&s_{v,i}\bt_{v,i}&\bp_{i}\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 3}, (16)
\bTi\displaystyle\bT_{i} =\bPi​\bMi.\displaystyle=\bPi\bM_{i}.

is Eq. (1) written as a matrix: it maps (u,v,1)⊤(u,v,1)^{\top} to the world point Pi​(u,v)P_{i}(u,v) in homogeneous form, (Pi​(u,v),1)⊤(P_{i}(u,v),1)^{\top}. It places the Hexel plane in the world. \bTi\bT_{i} is therefore the exact perspective map of the Hexel plane, whereas 3DGS [18] projects each Gaussian with a local affine approximation. Denote its rows by \btx⊤\bt_{x}^{\top}, \bty⊤\bt_{y}^{\top}, and \btz⊤\bt_{z}^{\top}. For a pixel (x,y)(x,y), define

\bk=x​\btz−\btx,\bl=y​\btz−\bty,𝐡=\bk×\bl.\bk=x\bt_{z}-\bt_{x},\qquad\bl=y\bt_{z}-\bt_{y},\qquad\mathbf{h}=\bk\times\bl. (17)

The intersection must satisfy \bk⊤​(u,v,1)⊤=\bl⊤​(u,v,1)⊤=0\bk^{\top}(u,v,1)^{\top}=\bl^{\top}(u,v,1)^{\top}=0. Since 𝐡\mathbf{h} is orthogonal to both \bk\bk and \bl\bl, the local coordinates are (u,v)=(hx/hz,hy/hz)(u,v)=(h_{x}/h_{z},h_{y}/h_{z}) when hz≠0h_{z}\neq 0. This recovers the perspective-correct intersection without a per-pixel matrix inverse. We skip intersections with hz=0h_{z}=0 or camera-space depth below the near-plane threshold of 0.20.2. Before Hexels are assigned to image tiles (see Visibility and compositing below), we also discard every Hexel whose center has camera-space depth at most 0.20.2. The same local coordinates are used to evaluate the hexagonal support and spatial color field.

Support bounds.

The sigmoid is nonzero outside the canonical hexagon, so we bound the region that can contribute above the rasterizer’s alpha threshold τ=1/255\tau=1/255. Since αi≤Ki\alpha_{i}\leq K_{i}, a contribution with αi≥τ\alpha_{i}\geq\tau must satisfy Ki≥τK_{i}\geq\tau. Substituting Ki=σ⁡(−βi​d)K_{i}=\sigma(-\beta_{i}d) gives

d⁡(u,v)≤1βi​log⁡1−ττ=log⁡254βi.d(u,v)\leq\frac{1}{\beta_{i}}\log\frac{1-\tau}{\tau}=\frac{\log 254}{\beta_{i}}. (18)

This defines a larger regular hexagon with center-to-edge distance 1+log⁡254/βi1+\log 254/\beta_{i}. It is enclosed by a circle with radius

ri=23​(1+log⁡254βi).r_{i}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\left(1+\frac{\log 254}{\beta_{i}}\right). (19)

The radius is in local Hexel coordinates, before tangent scaling and projection. We use this enclosing circle with the projective bounding routine inherited from 2DGS to determine the image tiles assigned to each primitive. The bound is conservative in the local plane because it uses the maximum possible opacity, rather than the learned opacity of each Hexel. The kernel computes a second, tighter box using the learned opacity. A contribution passes the threshold only if oi​Ki≥τo_{i}K_{i}\geq\tau, which holds only inside the smaller hexagon d⁡(u,v)≤βi−1​log⁡(oi/τ−1)d(u,v)\leq\beta_{i}^{-1}\log(o_{i}/\tau-1); a Hexel with oi<τo_{i}<\tau with oi<τo_{i}<\tau cannot contribute.

Visibility and compositing.

We divide the image into 16×1616\times 16-pixel tiles and assign each Hexel to the tiles intersecting its projected bound. Within each tile, primitives are sorted by their centers’ camera-space depth. This order is shared by the pixels in the tile; we do not sort intersections separately at each pixel.

For each candidate intersection, we evaluate its opacity as αi=min⁡{oi​Ki​(ui,vi),0.99}\alpha_{i}=\min\{o_{i}K_{i}(u_{i},v_{i}),0.99\} and skip contributions with αi<1/255\alpha_{i}<1/255. Let TT be the remaining transmittance before processing the candidate. If T⁡(1−αi)<10−4T(1-\alpha_{i})<10^{-4}, we stop without accumulating that candidate or updating TT. Otherwise, its color contribution is T​αi​\bci​(ui,vi,\bdi)T\alpha_{i}\bc_{i}(u_{i},v_{i},\bd_{i}), and we update T←T⁡(1−αi)T\leftarrow T(1-\alpha_{i}).

For the mm contributions actually accumulated at a pixel, indexed in their compositing order, the final color is

\bc​(\bx)\displaystyle\bc(\bx) =∑i=1mTi​αi​\bci​(ui,vi,\bdi)+Tend​\bcbg,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}T_{i}\alpha_{i}\bc_{i}(u_{i},v_{i},\bd_{i})+T_{\mathrm{end}}\bc_{\mathrm{bg}}, (20)
Ti\displaystyle T_{i} =∏j<i(1−αj),Tend=∏i=1m(1−αi).\displaystyle=\prod_{j<i}(1-\alpha_{j}),\qquad T_{\mathrm{end}}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1-\alpha_{i}).

Here \bcbg\bc_{\mathrm{bg}} is the background color. Its weight is the transmittance remaining after the contributions actually accumulated, not the tentative value that triggered early termination.

Appendix C Densification and Pruning

Hexels (V1/V2/V3 - Fixed) do not primarily use densification and pruning to avoid exceeding memory and/or primitive constraints in our primary experiments. Given our focus on practical efficiency, we want to avoid any hacks to improve our performance by temporarily going over the memory or primitive limits - which is why the peak VRAM values are very important, as often, other efficiency-focused methods do not report them. We, however, also report the densified NVS and surface reconstruction counterparts in our results - primarily in unconstrained settings - which are not the focus of our work. Notably, our baseline methods are allowed to temporarily exceed memory and primitive constraints to achieve better results, as they often perform much worse when forced to remain below these requirements.

Mixed growth.

Our densification strategy is similar to 3DGS and 2DGS. Between two growth triggers, for each Hexel, we track the norm of the loss gradient with respect to its projected 2D center, averaged over the iterations in which the Hexel is visible. A Hexel becomes a parent Hexel when this average is large, it was visible often enough, and it is not too young. Small parents are cloned, and large parents are split. A parent Hexel counts as small when its larger tangent scale is at most 1% of the scene extent. A clone is a copy of the parent Hexel whose center is moved within the parent’s tangent plane by a random Gaussian offset, scaled by the parent’s two scales. A split replaces the parent with two children, each offset randomly in the same plane, with both scales divided by 1.61.6, as in 3DGS, and an opacity ochild=1−1−oparento_{\mathrm{child}}=1-\sqrt{1-o_{\mathrm{parent}}}. New Hexels copy the parent’s appearance coefficients.

Contribution-based pruning.

Pruning removes Hexels that contribute very little to the scene. Each pruning session renders all training views 𝒱train\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{train}} and scores Hexel ii by its mean blending weight

qi=1|𝒱train|​∑v∈𝒱train1|Ωv|​∑\bx∈ΩvTi,v​(\bx)​αi,v​(\bx),q_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{train}}|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{train}}}\frac{1}{|\Omega_{v}|}\sum_{\bx\in\Omega_{v}}T_{i,v}(\bx)\alpha_{i,v}(\bx), (21)

where Ωv\Omega_{v} is the set of pixels of view vv and Ti,v​(\bx)​αi,v​(\bx)T_{i,v}(\bx)\alpha_{i,v}(\bx) is the weight of Hexel ii at pixel \bx\bx in Eq. (20). The weight is zero whenever the Hexel does not contribute – outside its tiles, below the alpha threshold, or after early termination. A Hexel can be pruned when qiq_{i} is below a threshold or has existed for longer than a grace period – this gives opportunity for newer Hexels to contribute.

Schedule and thresholds.

All densified (G) V1/V2/V3 models, for both NVS and surface reconstruction, use mixed growth every 500 iterations from 5.5K through 14.5K, with a ceiling of 2M Hexels. A parent Hexel needs an average gradient norm of at least 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, at least 20 observations since the previous growth trigger, and a minimum age of 500 iterations. Clone and split offsets have standard deviations of 0.250.25 and 0.50.5 times the parent’s scales, and a clone’s opacity is at most 0.020.02. Pruning runs every 1K iterations from 5K to 16K, with a 500-iteration grace period, a threshold of 10−710^{-7} on qiq_{i}, and at most 2% of the Hexels are removed per trigger. At each growth trigger, we also remove every Hexel with opacity below 0.0050.005, regardless of its age or the 2% limit. Opacities are never reset.

Appendix D 2D Image Representation

Hexels can represent an image directly by placing the primitives in the image plane. We retain the hexagonal support and first-order spatial color model, but replace 3D projection and depth-ordered compositing with image-space evaluation and blending.

Geometry and function support.

For a pixel \bx=(x,y)⊤\bx=(x,y)^{\top}, let \bmi=(mx,i,my,i)⊤\bm_{i}=(m_{x,i},m_{y,i})^{\top} be the Hexel center, \bR​(θi)\bR(\theta_{i}) its planar rotation, and \bSi=diag⁡(sx,i,sy,i)\bS_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(s_{x,i},s_{y,i}) its positive scale matrix. We compute local coordinates and the soft support weight (for numerical stability) \bS~i=\bSi+10−8​\bI2\widetilde{\bS}_{i}=\bS_{i}+10^{-8}\bI_{2}:

\bui​(\bx)=\bS~i−1​\bR​(θi)⊤​(\bmi−\bx),wi​(\bx)=σ⁡(−βi​d​(\bui​(\bx))),\bu_{i}(\bx)=\widetilde{\bS}_{i}^{-1}\bR(\theta_{i})^{\top}(\bm_{i}-\bx),\qquad w_{i}(\bx)=\sigma\!\left(-\beta_{i}d(\bu_{i}(\bx))\right), (22)

where dd is the hexagonal function from Eq. (2) and βi>0\beta_{i}>0 is the support sharpness. This evaluates the support directly at each pixel, without projection or ray–plane intersection. Since d⁡(\bu)=d⁡(−\bu)d(\bu)=d(-\bu), reversing the displacement does not change the support weight. Scales are optimized as log-scales. Hexels (V1) learn βi=softplus⁡(β~i)\beta_{i}=\operatorname{softplus}(\tilde{\beta}_{i}), initialized near 10; the constant-color ablation uses a fixed β=10\beta=10 shared by all primitives and not stored.

Spatial appearance.

We use the first-order spatial color model of V1, expressed here in image coordinates:

\bci​(\bx)=\bc0,i+η⁡[(mx,i−x)​\bgx,i+(my,i−y)​\bgy,i],\bc_{i}(\bx)=\bc_{0,i}+\eta\left[(m_{x,i}-x)\bg_{x,i}+(m_{y,i}-y)\bg_{y,i}\right], (23)

where \bc0,i\bc_{0,i} is the base RGB color, \bgx,i,\bgy,i∈ℝ3\bg_{x,i},\bg_{y,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} are the spatial color coefficients, and η=0.1\eta=0.1 controls their scale. The coefficients describe color changes along the image axes, using the center-minus-pixel displacement shown above. Unlike Eq. (4), these coordinates are not rotated or normalized by the Hexel scales. Both formulations represent an affine color field, but use different coordinate parameterizations. The constant-color ablation omits the two spatial terms, giving \bci​(\bx)=\bc0,i\bc_{i}(\bx)=\bc_{0,i}. Neither model uses view-dependent appearance.

Rendering.

Following Image-GS [40], we retain the K=10K=10 largest support weights among the primitives assigned to the pixel’s tile. Let 𝒮K​(\bx)\mathcal{S}_{K}(\bx) denote their indices. We blend their colors as

\bc​(\bx)=∑i∈𝒮K​(\bx)wi​(\bx)​\bci​(\bx)∑i∈𝒮K​(\bx)wi​(\bx)+ϵ,\bc(\bx)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{K}(\bx)}w_{i}(\bx)\bc_{i}(\bx)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{K}(\bx)}w_{i}(\bx)+\epsilon}, (24)

where ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4} prevents division by zero. Unlike the 3D compositor, this blend has no transmittance, depth ordering, or learned opacity: each retained primitive contributes according to its support weight relative to the others. During optimization, gradients propagate through the selected weights and colors to the Hexel parameters. The selected indices are treated as fixed when computing these gradients. Backward pass reuses the saved top-KK indices and reevaluates only their support weights and colors.

Finite support.

Each Hexel is assigned to the 16×1616\times 16 tiles overlapping a square of half-width ri=⌈23​max⁡(sx,i,sy,i)​(1+4.5/βi)⌉r_{i}=\lceil\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\max(s_{x,i},s_{y,i})(1+4.5/\beta_{i})\rceil pixels, which encloses the contour d=4.5/βid=4.5/\beta_{i} where wi=σ⁡(−4.5)≈0.011w_{i}=\sigma(-4.5)\approx 0.011. Every candidate in these tiles is evaluated without a weight threshold, and pixels in tiles without candidates are rendered as zero. Unlike the 3D bound of Eq. (18), this cutoff does not use 1/2551/255.

Experiment details.

We fit all 45 Image-GS images at 2048×20482048\times 2048 resolution for a primary 2D representation experiment. We use the Image-GS image-gradient initializer for both methods, with 30% sampled uniformly; base RGB values are sampled from the target image, scales are initialized at five pixels, while rotations and spatial color gradients are zero-initialized. Each Hexel is initialized with 20K primitives. From iterations 550 through 3000, we prune 200 primitives every 50 iterations, converging to 10K primitives. Hexels use L1 plus 0.1​(1−SSIM)0.1(1-\mathrm{SSIM}) loss and the Adam optimizer and stop early at 5100 iterations since Hexels converge faster. In a smaller experiment, we found that further training to 10,000 iterations did see marginal improvements in quality. All parameters and optimizer states are in FP32. For all methods in Table 1 same precision is used for all parameters. Memory size includes every active parameter and any relevant decoding metadata. Figure 3 uses values with the mean of three different experimental runs, with the variance spread displaying the differences in convergence across the entire Image-GS dataset.

Primitive Overdraw.

We distinguish the total number of primitives from the number covering each pixel. Since both Gaussian and Hexel supports have nonzero tails, we count a primitive as covering a pixel when its support weight reaches a common fraction τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1) of its own peak:

Cτ(\bx)=∑i=1N[wi​(\bx)max𝐲⁡wi​(𝐲)≥τ].C_{\tau}(\bx)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\frac{w_{i}(\bx)}{\max_{\mathbf{y}}w_{i}(\mathbf{y})}\geq\tau\right]. (25)

Here NN is the total primitive count and 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the indicator function. A value Cτ​(\bx)=0C_{\tau}(\bx)=0 means that no primitive covers the pixel at this threshold; Cτ​(\bx)=1C_{\tau}(\bx)=1 means that exactly one does, and larger values indicate overlapping supports. We count supports before top-KK selection, rather than summing the normalized blending weights. This measures spatial overlap that we refer to as overdraw.

We summarize coverage by the mean of CτC_{\tau} over the full image and the fractions of pixels covered by zero or multiple supports. A mean tending to one can result from uncovered pixels offsetting heavily overlapping regions. Primitive count and reconstruction quality are also reported for completeness. Comparing methods at matched reconstruction quality additionally tests whether Hexels require fewer primitives, rather than simply reducing overlap at the expense of quality.

Appendix E Implementation Details

E.1 Datasets and Metrics

We evaluate 34 scenes: nine from Mip-NeRF360, fifteen DTU scans (24, 37, 40, 55, 63, 65, 69, 83, 97, 105, 106, 110, 114, 118 and 122), and ten from Tanks and Temples (Barn, Caterpillar, Courthouse, Francis, Horse, Ignatius, Lighthouse, Meetingroom, Train and Truck). Every eighth camera is held out, with identical cameras and images across methods. Mip-NeRF360 uses quarter-resolution outdoor and half-resolution indoor images; DTU and T&T use half-resolution. PSNR and SSIM use float RGB images, and LPIPS-VGG inputs are normalized. We average reported metrics over test views, then equally over scenes for each configuration.

Colors rank methods within each primitive family and dataset. Teal and blue mark the best volumetric and hybrid values, respectively; red, orange, and yellow mark the top three surface values. F/G denote fixed/grown (densified) Hexels.

E.2 Initialization and Training

Hexels V1-V3 start from sparse COLMAP points and colors unless stated otherwise, with one Hexel per point and its color used as the base RGB point. Rotations start at identity quaternion initialization, without estimated surface normals. Both tangent scales are initialized to one quarter of the root-mean-square distance to the three nearest neighbors, capped at 5% of the scene camera extent. Opacity is initialized at 0.1 and sharpness parameter at 10. Spatial color gradients and view-dependent coefficients are initialized to zero. We optimize geometry, opacity, sharpness, and appearance parameters jointly. We train using Adam optimizer for 30K iterations using the photometric loss and with SSIM weight 0.2. Experiments using densification, usually in the unconstrained case, use the method described in Appendix C. Unlike some other baselines, for NVS experiments, Hexels do not use depth distortion, normal regularization, or MVS initialization. Details regarding learning rates are given in Table 7.

2D image fitting.

For the image-representation experiments, Hexels use following learning rates: 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} for centers, 10−210^{-2} for (log-)scales, 2×10−32\times 10^{-3} for rotation angles, 5×10−35\times 10^{-3} for base RGB, and 10−310^{-3} for spatial RGB gradients and support-sharpness parameters when present. All rates are reduced tenfold at iteration 5001. Hexels stop at 5100 iterations after pruning from 20K to 10K primitives, as detailed in Appendix D. Image-GS retains its original parameterization and hyperparameters.

E.3 Baseline Settings

We use the authors’ implementations of 2DGS, 3DGS, 3D Convex Splatting, Triangle Splatting, BBSplat, MeshSplatting, and Nexels. BBSplat trains for 32K iterations and includes compressed textures to reduce reported memory requirements post hoc.

Reported model memory, including matched model memory experiments, includes all primitive and appearance parameters, including textures, feature grids and decoders. Nexels use a reduced feature grid to fit within each experimental budget. MeshSplatting is matched at initialization; native remeshing can change its final memory. Matched-primitive experiments limit final populations to the scene’s SfM point count while retaining native growth and pruning. Native comparisons use each baseline’s original population policy.

For DTU surface reconstruction experiment, native unconstrained and budget-controlled 2DGS use normal-consistency and depth-distortion loss weights of 0.05 and 1000, respectively. For the constrained experiments, the Hexels primitive or model-memory budget determines the final population ceiling; after initialization and each densification/pruning update, we retain the highest-opacity primitives up to that ceiling. This means that during densification, 2dGS can and does go beyond the set primitive limits - we note that if these limits are used strictly, 2DGS and other baselines perform poorly. This further shows that Hexels, which actually do strictly conform to the memory or primitive budgets, usually without doing densification, are state-of-the-art or surface line primitives in terms of efficiency-quality frontier.

E.4 Timing and Memory

Hardware and rendering speed.

Experiments use RTX A5000 GPUs; starred rows are experiments that were run on RTX 6000 Ada as A5000 memory was insufficient for that specific experiment. For FPS calculations, we perform two warmup passes and run four trials of ten passes across all test camera viewpoints, with GPU synchronization. We report the median FPS per scene and average over scenes, excluding loading, image transfer, and metric computation.

2D image fitting/training timing.

The 2D fitting times include optimization and pruning, excluding initialization, evaluation and any post-hoc I/O. For Table 1, all three stored representations are decoded and timed using the same A5000 rendering protocol: 10 warmup renders followed by 5 trials of 20 renders, with GPU synchronization. We take the median latency per image, convert it to FPS, and average equally over all 45 images. These repeated renders of a single image measure rendering throughput, excluding file I/O.

Model memory and deployment size.

Model memory is the memory of the uncompressed model used for inference: all FP32 parameters needed for rendering, without optimizer state. Hexels V1/V2/V3 use 80/116/260 bytes per primitive. Deployment size includes files needed for inference, including configuration and appearance parameters, in decimal MB. NVS comparison tables report the original uncompressed FP32 inference files; compression for deployment is evaluated separately in Appendix I.3.

Training resources.

Peak VRAM is the sampled process GPU memory during training, in GiB; dataset values average the per-scene peaks. Training time includes initialization, optimization and checkpoint saving, but excludes separate evaluation, compression, and video generation. For VRAM calculation, we run multiple runs and sample GPU memory at approximately 2 ms or 5 ms intervals using NVIDIA’s NVML API. All mean text VRAM calculations use this, while some in the appendix may use just 5ms sampling.

E.5 Hexel Surface-Cell Representation

A Hexel can be used to specify a hexagonal cell through d⁡(u,v)=0d(u,v)=0 in Eq. (2). The six vertices can be mapped analytically into the world space through Eq. (1). Importantly, this is differentiable and can be done in constant time per Hexel or any other polygonal primitive with low overdraw. However, this might not be possible for the more prevalent Gaussian-based surfels like 2DGS. A Gaussian surfel [14] has a smooth local representation G(u,v)=exp[−(u2+v2)/2]G(u,v)=\exp[-(u^{2}+v^{2})/2], with no explicitly finite boundary; therefore, getting such a differentiable, constant-time surface cell representation is non-trivial.

E.6 Spatial Appearance Ablations

Tables 14 and 15 compare all six Hexels configurations (V1/V2/V3 with fixed or densified populations) on Mip-NeRF360, DTU, and Tanks and Temples. V3 with densification achieves the highest PSNR across all three datasets. Fixed population variants require less memory and render faster. Densification improves V3’s PSNR on Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks and Temples; on DTU, fixed V3 achieves slightly higher PSNR (29.95 versus 29.76 dB), whereas densified V3 improves LPIPS (0.268 versus 0.293).

Appendix F Surface Reconstruction Ablations

In this section, we perform ablations on the Hexels’ model underlying our DTU surface reconstruction results in Table 5: a fixed-population V3 model initialized from multi-view stereo (MVS) points and trained with the normal-consistency and depth-distortion losses, similar to 2DGS. Starting with this configuration, we change one group of choices at a time.

  • •

    Surface losses (Table 8(a)): we drop normal consistency, depth distortion, or both.

  • •

    Initialization (Table 8(a)): we start from sparse structure-from-motion (SfM) points instead of MVS points.

  • •

    Appearance and population (Table 8(b)): keeping both losses, we train V1, V2, and V3 from SfM or MVS points, each with a fixed population or with the densification and pruning of Appendix C.

Every experiment uses the same 15 DTU scans, all registered training views, 30,000 training iterations, with the same TSDF extraction and official DTU evaluation. Chamfer distance (CD) is the mean of accuracy and completeness, measured in millimeters and averaged over scans. When enabled, the normal-consistency and depth-distortion weights are 0.05 and 1000, respectively.

Surface losses.

Table 8(a) reports 1.575 mm CD without either loss, 1.246 mm with depth distortion alone, 0.986 mm with normal consistency alone and 0.978 mm with both losses. Normal consistency provides the larger individual improvement, with a smaller complementary benefit from depth distortion.

Initialization.

For fixed V3 with both losses enabled, MVS initialization reduces mean CD from 1.146 mm for structure-from-motion (SfM) initialization to 0.978 mm, a 14.6% reduction at unchanged primitive count and model memory.

Appearance and population.

In Table 8(b), V3 has the lowest CD with either setting of initialization or population, and MVS initialization beats SfM for every variant. Densification improves CD in 5 out of 6 appearance mode and initialization pairs; the only exception is V3 with SfM (1.146 mm fixed versus 1.193 mm densified). Densified V3 from MVS has the lowest CD overall (0.922 mm), but it needs 33.17 MB model memory vs 8.83 MB in the fixed variant, so the memory-matched comparison in Table 5 uses fixed V3. Figures 10 and 11 show the runs of Table 8(a) and (b) on DTU scan24.

Unconstrained surface reconstruction.

We additionally evaluate the methods without a matched memory budget. Native 2DGS achieves lower DTU CD than Hexels (0.794 mm), but Hexels remains competitive (0.978 mm) while requiring substantially less model memory and training resources (1.93 GiB VRAM for 2DGS vs. 0.61 GiB for Hexels). On Tanks and Temples, Hexels has higher mean F1 (34.38% versus 31.72%). Figure 12 provides additional qualitative results. The zoomed crops show holes in Triangle Splatting’s skull and pedestal surfaces and spurious sheets above the ‘Caterpillar’ cab in the memory-matched 2DGS results. Hexels reduces these artifacts in the displayed regions.

Appendix G Why Hexagons and Spatial Color?

We want each Hexel to represent a large surface region without losing the appearance variation inside it. This requires two choices: a shape that can cover surfaces efficiently, and a color model that can describe more than a constant color. The honeycomb theorem motivates the first choice: regular hexagons minimize boundary length among equal-area partitions of the plane [9]. The spatial color field addresses the second.

We examine these choices on one planar patch at a fixed viewing direction. First, we show that an affine color field represents the local color slope, with the remaining error controlled by how that slope changes across the patch. This determines a region where one color field stays within a chosen error tolerance. We then show that, within the same region, the largest affine hexagon covers twice the area of the largest affine triangle and about 30% more than the largest affine square.

G.1 Linear Color

We fix a viewing direction and use orthonormal coordinates \bx∈ℝ2\bx\in\mathbb{R}^{2} on a localized plane. Let \bp\bp be the patch center and \bh=\bx−\bp\bh=\bx-\bp. In axes aligned with the primitive, \bh=(su​u,sv​v)⊤\bh=(s_{u}u,s_{v}v)^{\top}, where (u,v)(u,v) are its normalized local coordinates.

Let ff be one target color (channel). An affine color field represents a constant and a linear change in color. The remaining approximation error depends on the second derivatives of ff, which describe how its slope changes across the patch. We are assuming a standard local approximation argument underlying piecewise-polynomial representations  [3].

Proposition G.1 (Local error of an affine color field).

Let ff be twice continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood UU containing \bp\bp. Suppose a fixed symmetric positive-definite matrix \bQ\bQ satisfies

|\bz⊤​D2​f​(\bx)​\bz|≤\bz⊤​\bQ​\bzfor all \bx∈U,\bz∈ℝ2.|\bz^{\top}D^{2}f(\bx)\bz|\leq\bz^{\top}\bQ\bz\qquad\text{for all }\bx\in U,\ \bz\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. (26)

Then, for every \bp+\bh∈U\bp+\bh\in U, the affine field ℓ\bp(\bp+\bh)=f(\bp)+∇f(\bp)⊤\bh\ell_{\bp}(\bp+\bh)=f(\bp)+\nabla f(\bp)^{\top}\bh satisfies

|f⁡(\bp+\bh)−ℓ\bp​(\bp+\bh)|≤12​\bh⊤​\bQ​\bh.|f(\bp+\bh)-\ell_{\bp}(\bp+\bh)|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\bh^{\top}\bQ\bh. (27)

In particular, if ‖D2​f​(\bx)‖op≤M\|D^{2}f(\bx)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq M throughout UU, the error is at most M​r2/2Mr^{2}/2 wherever ‖\bh‖≤r\|\bh\|\leq r.

Proof G.2.

Define g⁡(t)=f⁡(\bp+t​\bh)g(t)=f(\bp+t\bh) for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus twice gives

f⁡(\bp+\bh)−ℓ\bp​(\bp+\bh)\displaystyle f(\bp+\bh)-\ell_{\bp}(\bp+\bh) =∫01(1−t)​g′′​(t)​dt,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)g^{\prime\prime}(t)\,dt, (28)
g′′​(t)\displaystyle g^{\prime\prime}(t) =\bh⊤​D2​f​(\bp+t​\bh)​\bh.\displaystyle=\bh^{\top}D^{2}f(\bp+t\bh)\bh.

The segment lies in UU, so Eq. (26) gives

|f⁡(\bp+\bh)−ℓ\bp​(\bp+\bh)|\displaystyle|f(\bp+\bh)-\ell_{\bp}(\bp+\bh)| ≤∫01(1−t)​|\bh⊤​D2​f​(\bp+t​\bh)​\bh|​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\left|\bh^{\top}D^{2}f(\bp+t\bh)\bh\right|\,dt (29)
≤\bh⊤​\bQ​\bh​∫01(1−t)​dt=12​\bh⊤​\bQ​\bh.\displaystyle\leq\bh^{\top}\bQ\bh\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\,dt=\tfrac{1}{2}\bh^{\top}\bQ\bh.

The operator-norm statement follows by replacing the quadratic-form bound with M​‖\bh‖2M\|\bh\|^{2}.

The affine field therefore accounts for the local slope, leaving an error controlled by changes in that slope. In comparison, using only the constant value f⁡(\bp)f(\bp) gives an error bound of L​rLr when ‖∇f‖≤L\|\nabla f\|\leq L. A nonconstant affine color ramp is represented exactly by the affine field, but not by one constant color. This compares individual color fields; blending constant-color primitives can also produce spatial variation.

The Hexel spatial field contains this Taylor approximation. For one color channel, in primitive-aligned physical coordinates, the required coefficients are

c0=f⁡(\bp),gu=su​∂1f⁡(\bp),gv=sv​∂2f⁡(\bp).c_{0}=f(\bp),\qquad g_{u}=s_{u}\,\partial_{1}f(\bp),\qquad g_{v}=s_{v}\,\partial_{2}f(\bp). (30)

Substituting these into c0+u​gu+v​gvc_{0}+ug_{u}+vg_{v} gives ℓ\bp​(\bp+\bh)\ell_{\bp}(\bp+\bh). Normalized local coordinates therefore change the coefficients, not the class of affine functions that can be represented.

For RGB, apply the same argument to each channel using a common matrix \bQ\bQ. Let 𝐟\mathbf{f} be the target RGB field and ℓ\bp\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\bp} its channel-wise Taylor approximation. For a learned field 𝐂\mathbf{C}, define η⁡(\bx)=‖𝐂⁡(\bx)−ℓ\bp​(\bx)‖∞\eta(\bx)=\|\mathbf{C}(\bx)-\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\bp}(\bx)\|_{\infty}. Then

‖𝐂⁡(\bp+\bh)−𝐟⁡(\bp+\bh)‖∞≤η⁡(\bp+\bh)+12​\bh⊤​\bQ​\bh.\|\mathbf{C}(\bp+\bh)-\mathbf{f}(\bp+\bh)\|_{\infty}\leq\eta(\bp+\bh)+\tfrac{1}{2}\bh^{\top}\bQ\bh. (31)

Here ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} is the largest absolute RGB-channel error. The term η\eta accounts for the difference between the learned field and the Taylor field. The result establishes the available approximation capacity, rather than assuming that optimization reaches the Taylor coefficients.

G.2 Patch Shape

For a tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0, define

E={\bp+\bh:\bh⊤​\bQ​\bh≤2​ε}.E=\{\bp+\bh:\bh^{\top}\bQ\bh\leq 2\varepsilon\}. (32)

Provided E⊂UE\subset U, the Taylor color error is at most ε\varepsilon throughout this ellipse. Its longer directions allow larger displacements while satisfying the same error bound. The matrix \bQ\bQ bounds changes in color slope; it is not a surface curvature matrix and is not estimated by our training procedure.

The regular triangle, square, and hexagon each tile the plane. We now compare their affine images inside the same error ellipse: how much area can each patch cover while satisfying the same Taylor color-error bound?

Proposition G.3 (Patch area within one error ellipse).

Let HmH_{m} be a filled regular mm-gon centered at the origin, with m≥3m\geq 3 and unit circumradius. Among all translated, nonsingular affine images of HmH_{m} contained in EE, the maximum area is

Ammax=m​sin⁡(2​π/m)​εdet\bQ.A_{m}^{\max}=\frac{m\sin(2\pi/m)\,\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\det\bQ}}. (33)

A maximizer is \bp+2​ε\bQ−1/2\bRHm\bp+\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\,\bQ^{-1/2}\bR H_{m}, where \bR\bR is any orthogonal matrix. Consequently,

Connection to the Hexel parameterization.

The maximizing hexagon can be represented using the rotation and two tangent scales already present in Hexels. Write \bQ=\bU​diag⁡(λ1,λ2)​\bU⊤\bQ=\bU\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})\bU^{\top}, where λ1,λ2>0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0 and the eigenvectors in \bU\bU are chosen to form a rotation. Align the tangent axes with these eigenvectors. Since our canonical hexagon has inradius one and circumradius 2/32/\sqrt{3}, choose

su=3​ε2​λ1,sv=3​ε2​λ2.s_{u}=\sqrt{\frac{3\varepsilon}{2\lambda_{1}}},\qquad s_{v}=\sqrt{\frac{3\varepsilon}{2\lambda_{2}}}. (38)

This places the six vertices on the error ellipse and attains A6maxA_{6}^{\max}.

Thus, among affine images of these three regular tiling cells, the hexagon covers the largest area inside the same sufficient color-error ellipse. Combined with the tiling motivation, this supports using a hexagonal patch with an affine color field: one element can represent a larger region than the corresponding triangular or square element under this local approximation bound.

G.3 3D Alpha Compositing

The preceding results concern the color represented within individual patches. In 3D rendering, the final pixel also depends on alpha compositing and the remaining background transmittance.

Proposition G.5 (Error under alpha compositing).

At one pixel, let 0≤αi≤10\leq\alpha_{i}\leq 1 be a finite ordered list of retained contributions, with colors CiC_{i}. Define

‖I−f‖≤∑iwi​‖Ci−f‖+T​‖b−f‖.\|I-f\|\leq\sum_{i}w_{i}\|C_{i}-f\|+T\|b-f\|. (40)
