Appendix H Extended Related Work

Novel view synthesis and surface reconstruction.

NeRF [25] was introduced for novel view synthesis and represents a scene as a neural field of density and view-dependent radiance. This representation enabled high-quality novel-view rendering. However, the repeated network evaluations required for volumetric rendering made the original NeRF expensive to train and slow to render. A large body of follow-up work introduced explicit feature grids, hash encodings, precomputed representations, and baked representations to reduce the sampling, rendering, and computational demands of the original neural-field models [26, 6, 28].

3DGS [18] introduced an alternative for substantially more efficient rendering using explicit anisotropic Gaussian volume primitives, enabling real-time rasterization. However, because of their volumetric nature, 3D Gaussians are not naturally surface aligned and can produce inaccurate geometry. To remedy this, works such as SuGaR [7] regularize Gaussians toward surfaces. An important solution was introduced by 2DGS [14], which instead represents the scene using oriented planar Gaussian surfels and perspective-correct ray–plane intersections, retaining fast rasterization while substantially improving the geometry.

Despite the large improvements made by 3DGS and 2DGS in training and rendering time relative to NeRF, these improvements are still not enough for truly resource-constrained settings. Efficiency requires several things at the same time: learned model storage and training VRAM should be as low as possible, primitive count should remain small relative to the cost of each primitive, and the representation should still retain high reconstruction quality and fast rendering. 3DGS and 2DGS can both require large primitive populations and substantial memory. Despite this, we find that 2DGS remains the strongest prior native surface representation in terms of the overall performance–efficiency balance when these factors are considered together, even after a number of subsequent works have attempted to improve different parts of the problem.

Primitive-based differentiable rendering.

Different follow-up works have tried to make the primitive more expressive, reduce the number of primitives, increase rendering speed, reduce model storage, or address limitations of 2DGS and earlier Gaussian representations, such as the infinite support of Gaussian kernels. GES [10], for example, replaces the Gaussian with a more flexible generalized exponential kernel, while Deformable Beta Splatting [23] introduces bounded and deformable kernels. 3D Convex Splatting [11] instead uses smooth 3D convex primitives, allowing more flexible volumetric geometry and sharper boundaries, but remains a volumetric rather than surface-aligned representation.

Triangle Splatting [13], on the other hand, optimizes an independent triangle soup so that high rendering speeds can be achieved while retaining a surface-aligned primitive. However, high-quality scenes can still require very large triangle populations, increasing both model storage and the computation and memory required during optimization. The independent triangle soup also does not provide surface connectivity. MeshSplatting [12] follows this work by introducing explicit connectivity and an opaque mesh representation, trading the independence of individual splats for a conventional connected surface. Other works increase geometric complexity in different ways, including Quadratic Gaussian Splatting [41], which introduces curved patches, and MILo [8], which brings mesh construction directly into Gaussian optimization. In our experiments, we focus on 2DGS, Triangle Splatting, and MeshSplatting, which we find provide the strongest overall quality–efficiency trade-offs among prior native surface-aligned representations.

Hexels are also primitive-based renderers, but we try to solve a more fundamental problem: can we design a more efficient primitive that is able to exploit the structure found in the world, both in geometry and appearance? Like 2DGS, we retain independent planar elements, but change the region represented by one element and the signal represented inside it. We use an affine hexagonal patch, which gives a large, nearly isotropic local region, together with a first-order color field that models smooth appearance variation across a surface. We find that much of the variation on local surfaces is smooth, making such a representation particularly efficient.

A first-order color field, by itself, is not unique to Hexels: a vertex-colored triangle (another tiling primitive), for example, can also represent an affine color field. The domain of our primitive, however, makes an important difference. Under the same local approximation-error ellipse, our analysis shows that the largest admissible affine regular hexagon can cover twice the area of the corresponding affine triangle and about 1.3×1.3\times that of the square (Appendix G). Hexels therefore increase the amount represented by a simple planar element without requiring complex geometry, volumetric convexes, or mesh connectivity.

Hybrid primitives and representations.

The most direct comparisons to Hexels are fundamentally native surface primitives. However, there has also been a trend toward hybrid representations that separate geometry from appearance in order to improve particular aspects of efficiency over 2DGS-like representations. Gaussian Billboards [35], for example, introduces spatially varying appearance through per-splat texture interpolation. BBSplat [33] learns separate RGB and alpha texture maps to reduce the number of geometric primitives required. This can substantially reduce primitive count, but the textures themselves become part of the model and training cost. NeST [39] follows a related idea by separating sparse surface geometry from a neural appearance representation. Nexels  [30] similarly combines sparse surfels with a shared neural appearance field and per-primitive colors. These methods can substantially reduce geometric primitive count, but this capacity is moved into texture maps, feature fields, or neural networks, which introduce additional memory, training state, and computation. Concurrent work such as Bake It Till You Make It [17], which is also centered on improving the efficiency of surface splats, follows this hybrid direction. It uses sparse surface geometry together with a hash-based appearance representation during optimization, and later bakes high-frequency appearance into a texture atlas for rendering. This can reduce the number of geometric surface primitives and improve rendering speed, but appearance is again moved outside the primitive and requires a separate representation and baking pipeline.

These ideas of separating geometry and appearance, neural textures, and texture baking are interesting, but they can in principle be applied on top of different native surface primitives. They also often come with a different set of trade-offs, be it slower rendering, more memory or non-ideal decoupled optimization. They therefore answer a somewhat different question from ours. We include these methods in our comparisons, but count their full learned representation, including textures, feature grids, and neural decoders, rather than only the number of geometric elements. These hybrid setups, however, are not the objective of our work.

Population control and compression.

Given the multifaceted nature of the efficiency problem, another body of work has developed around interventions on existing primitives to improve different aspects of their efficiency. Scaffold-GS [24], for example, reduces 3DGS redundancy through anchors that generate view-adaptive Gaussian attributes rather than storing every Gaussian independently. 3DGS-MCMC [19] improves primitive allocation through stochastic updates and relocation. FastGS  [29] instead focuses on training time, using multi-view-consistent densification and pruning to reduce unnecessary Gaussian growth.

A related line of work compresses already learned representations. LightGaussian [5] prunes low-importance Gaussians, distills appearance into lower-order spherical harmonics, and applies vector quantization to reduce model size. Compact 3D Gaussian Representation [22] combines learnable masking with shared neural appearance, vector quantization, and entropy coding. Compressed 3DGS [27] similarly uses quantization-aware clustering and codebooks to reduce storage. Related ideas have also been developed for surface-based Gaussian representations.

These methods are useful and complementary, but they start with an already chosen primitive and add additional methodology around it. They may greatly improve one aspect of efficiency without necessarily reducing the memory and computation required elsewhere, particularly during training. Our focus is therefore the more fundamental question: we can add pruning, quantization, codebooks, texture atlases, neural decoders, and other post-hoc compression, but can we also start with a more efficient native surface primitive? Hexels address this question before these additional techniques are applied; many of them could still be applied on top of Hexels afterward.

Neural Image Representations.

A similar line of research has developed independently in 2D, where neural image representations are used to encode visual media. Earlier approaches often relied on autoencoders or implicit neural functions. More recently, GaussianImage [38] adapted ideas from Gaussian splatting to represent images using simple 2D Gaussian primitives, demonstrating fast fitting and rendering. Image-GS [40] further improves this representation using content-adaptive initialization and progressive optimization of anisotropic 2D Gaussians. SAD [15] instead represents the image through a soft anisotropic partition whose regions depend on neighboring sites rather than independently parameterized primitives. We compare Hexels primarily with Image-GS because both use independently parameterized image primitives, enabling a direct comparison of quality and efficiency per primitive. SAD instead represents images through a coupled partition whose regions depend on neighboring sites, addressing a different representation regime that we leave for future comparison.

We show that Hexels can also be used directly for 2D image representation, where they outperform Image-GS in reconstruction quality and training convergence under our evaluated settings. More importantly, Hexels are designed as a general surface primitive rather than separate 2D and 3D representations. In 2D, the primitive is placed directly in the image plane; in 3D, it is oriented on a surface patch. While the compositor changes where required by visibility and depth ordering, the basic hexagonal support and appearance model remain the same. This gives Hexels a general capability across image representation, novel-view synthesis, and surface reconstruction, rather than requiring a separate representation for each setting.

Overall efficiency.

A common pattern across methods that have tried to make surface-aligned representations more efficient is that the cost is often moved to another part of the problem. Faster rasterization may still require a very large primitive population. Sparse geometry may move capacity into external texture maps or neural fields, increasing representation complexity, training VRAM, or final model storage. Compression can make the deployed scene small while having much less effect on the size and memory required during training. Richer geometry can reduce primitive count while increasing the cost of each primitive.

Hexels are designed to alleviate these problems together, without first resorting to post-hoc retrofitting and before pruning or compression is applied. We use the fact that natural images, surfaces, and scenes contain local structure. Large regions are often approximately planar and vary smoothly in appearance. A Hexel covers a bounded, efficient local region and models first-order appearance variation inside it, allowing simple regions to be represented by larger and fewer elements. This allows us to target high quality, low learned storage, low training VRAM, few primitives, and high FPS in the same native surface representation, in both 2D and 3D. Pruning, quantization, neural appearance models, and other post-hoc improvements remain possible additions rather than requirements of the representation.

Appendix I Full NVS Results

We report additional model-memory experiments, all six Hexels configurations (V1, V2, V3 fixed and densified), initial compression results, and per-scene results on the 34-scene benchmark. FF stands for fixed primitives from SfM initialization whereas GG stands for their densified counterparts, unless stated otherwise.

I.1 Matched Model Memory

At the V2 memory budget, Hexels exceeds Triangle Splatting by 1.40 dB outdoors and 2.19 dB indoors on Mip-NeRF360 (Table 9). On DTU, it renders at 1.65×1.65\times Triangle’s mean FPS (Table 10). At the V3 budget, the PSNR gains over Triangle are 0.54/0.55 dB on outdoor/indoor Mip-NeRF360 (Table 11) and 2.73/0.83 dB on DTU/T&T (Table 12). Across these V2/V3 budgets, Hexels has higher PSNR than MeshSplatting across all 3 datasets, with higher SSIM and lower LPIPS. Table 13 lists the model-memory budgets for each scene.

I.2 Fixed and Densified Hexels

Densifying V3 improves PSNR by 1.37 dB outdoors and 0.78 dB indoors on Mip-NeRF360 (Table 14), increasing deployment size from 17.0 to 337.6 MB and 48.2 to 133.2 MB, respectively. On DTU, densified V3 has 0.20 dB lower PSNR than fixed V3 but 0.026 lower LPIPS; on T&T it gains 0.76 dB (Table 15). Fixed models therefore offer a particularly compact option for DTU, while growth improves quality on the larger scenes.

I.3 Deployment Compression analysis

While outside our core efficiency objectives, we also provide an initial analysis of lossless compression and appearance parameter quantization (PQ1024) on all six variants across 34 scenes. Our lossless compression analysis keeps every FP32 parameter exact. It regroups the bytes of each parameter array by position (all first bytes of the 4-byte values, then all second bytes, and so on), so that the highly repetitive sign and exponent bytes are stored together. It then compresses the result with DEFLATE [4], the standard LZ77 and Huffman-coding compressor used by ZIP and gzip software. PQ1024 replaces RGB appearance vectors with 1,024-entry codebooks: one per SH coefficient for V3, and corresponding codebooks for the spatial and directional gradients of V1/V2. Geometry and base color remain lossless. Parameters are decoded to FP32 before rendering, without retraining.

Lossless compression and PQ1024 evaluated here are additional experiments; the main NVS experiments use uncompressed FP32 models. Quantizing V2 reduces PSNR by \val0.55–0.61dB, whereas densifier V3-G PQ1024 changes mean PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS by −0.01674-0.01674 dB/−0.000259-0.000259/+0.000849+0.000849 (Table 16). The largest dataset-mean PSNR loss for V3-G is 0.0303 dB on Mip-NeRF360. Across 34 scenes, its mean deployment size is 43.87 MB, 60.09% below lossless compression. Table 16 reports these compressed results whereas all other NVS comparison tables use uncompressed FP32 representation.

Encoding time includes codebook fitting; decoding measures cached reading and CPU-based reconstruction, followed by upload into an allocated model.

2D model size (deployment) compression.

For the 2D representation in Table 1, mixed-bit storage reduces mean PSNR by 0.03307 dB for constant-color Hexels and 0.01091 dB for linear-color Hexels relative to their FP32 parameters.

After training/image fitting, constant-color Hexels store positions, (log-)scales, rotations and RGB parameters with 16, 14, 12 and 10 bits per scalar, respectively. Linear-color Hexels use 16, 14, 12, 12, 14 and 10 bits for positions, scales, rotations, base RGB, spatial RGB gradients and sharpness. The bit-packed files include a 1024-byte header containing quantization ranges and decoder settings. At 10K primitives, the constant and linear files occupy 128524 and 253524 bytes, or 0.2451 and 0.4836 bits per pixel. The 16-bit Image-GS files occupy 161024 bytes, or 0.3071 bits per pixel. Both Hexel variants show similar performance for 16-bit storage: at most 0.05 dB mean PSNR loss, 0.2 dB worst-image loss, and 0.001 mean SSIM loss on the evaluated samples.
